findings: No sustained arrhythmia. No pauses greater than 2 seconds. No AV block.

csf.interpretation: Unremarkable CSF. Normal cell count, protein, and glucose.

ct.impression: No acute intracranial abnormality. No haemorrhage, mass, hydrocephalus, or large-territory infarct.

findings: Structurally normal heart. No intracardiac thrombus or vegetation. No pericardial effusion.

citations: Daum C et al. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2014;85:180-190
action_criteria.expected_evidence: Give-way leg weakness, tremor that entrains and stops with distraction; Hoover equivocal; normal reflexes and plantars
action_criteria.label: Examine for positive functional signs
action_criteria.rationale: The examination makes the diagnosis of the weakness and tremor: collapsing weakness, entrainment and distractibility are positive signs, while normal tone, reflexes and plantar responses after 8 months argue against myelopathy or motor neuron disease. An equivocal Hoover sign does not negate them.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Habitual events recorded on video with no EEG change and a normal interictal record
action_criteria.label: Video-EEG to record the habitual events
action_criteria.rationale: Recording the habitual shaking events on video-EEG without ictal change reaches the ILAE documented level of certainty; events occur 2-3 times a week, so capturing one takes prolonged inpatient monitoring, and the record also screens for co-occurring epilepsy (AAN 2025). Without the recording, the positive signs and the semiology of witnessed events support the diagnosis at a lower ILAE level of certainty (LaFrance 2013).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Serotonergic combination of an SNRI, a triptan and cyclobenzaprine, sedative load, and SNRI-NSAID bleeding risk
action_criteria.label: Medication review
action_criteria.rationale: Duloxetine, cyclobenzaprine and sumatriptan form a serotonergic combination that can itself cause tremor and clonus; pregabalin and cyclobenzaprine add sedation and imbalance; duloxetine with ibuprofen raises bleeding risk.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Profile of comorbid mood, anxiety and somatic symptom burden to guide therapy; no bearing on the diagnosis
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological assessment of mood, anxiety and dissociation
action_criteria.rationale: A battery with performance-validity measures can characterise the comorbidity that treatment will target; it does not make the diagnosis and is the most expensive item on this pathway.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Background evidence only; the diagnosis and plan for this patient do not depend on a literature result
action_criteria.label: Search the literature on functional neurological disorder
action_criteria.rationale: General evidence on positive diagnosis and treatment can inform the explanation and the referral; no step of the diagnostic work-up depends on it.

prohibited_recommendations: Order further investigations once the positive diagnosis is established, without a new specific clinical question (repeat brain or spine MRI, repeat nerve conduction studies or EMG, CT, lumbar puncture, evoked potentials, PET).
Tell the patient the symptoms are imagined, feigned, 'all in your head', or that nothing is wrong.
Perform invasive testing without a specific indication (lumbar puncture, nerve or muscle biopsy, catheter angiography).
Start or escalate antiseizure medication for the functional seizures.
Give benzodiazepines or intubate for a typical functional seizure.
Give gadolinium contrast without a specific indication.
required_recommendations: Make a positive diagnosis of functional neurological disorder (mixed: functional leg weakness, functional tremor and functional seizures) based on collapsing leg weakness, tremor entrainment and distractibility, and the semiology of the habitual events, confirmed on video-EEG where recorded, and not by exclusion of other disease.

Explain the diagnosis to the patient, and with consent to the family, as a common and genuine disorder of nervous system functioning that can improve, show the positive signs, and give written information.
Refer for physiotherapy with expertise in functional motor disorder (motor retraining, Nielsen 2015 consensus).
Refer for psychological therapy by a clinician experienced in FND (CBT-informed) and treat the comorbid depression and generalized anxiety disorder.

Give the patient, family and ward a written plan for typical events: keep safe, do not restrain, wait for the event to end, and do not give emergency benzodiazepines or intubate for a typical functional seizure.

avoided_actions.rationale: No cardiac symptom or murmur; the events keep awareness and have no syncopal features.
Her events are prolonged shaking with retained awareness, not syncope; a rhythm recording answers no question.
A normal brain and spine MRI was already obtained; a CT adds radiation and no information.
Normal reflexes, plantar responses and outpatient MRI give a lumbar puncture no question to answer; it is invasive and reinforces the search for an organic cause.
No metabolic or neurodegenerative question: the weakness and tremor show positive functional signs.
Nerve conduction studies were already normal as an outpatient; repeating them or adding EMG answers no question and a normal result reinforces the search for an organic cause.
Evoked potentials cannot explain a non-dermatomal sensory loss with a midline split, which is not a pathway lesion.
A normal brain and spine MRI was obtained as an outpatient; repeating it answers no new question (Stone 2016).
The outpatient spine MRI was normal, and normal tone, reflexes and plantar responses give no new myelopathy question; repeating it reinforces illness conviction.

accepted: Functional neurological disorder (conversion disorder) with weakness, abnormal movements (functional tremor), and psychogenic non-epileptic seizures

differential.key_features: Habitual events recorded on video-EEG without ictal change; co-occurring epilepsy remains possible in about one in five patients with functional seizures.

Raised by the referral and a maternal aunt with MS; normal tone, reflexes and flexor plantar responses after 8 months, positive functional signs, and the normal outpatient brain and spine MRI argue against it.
Raised by the referral; no atrophy, fasciculations or reflex change after 8 months of severe weakness, and prominent sensory symptoms.

Duloxetine can cause tremor, but her tremor varies in frequency, entrains to tapping of the other hand and stops with distraction, which a drug-induced, essential or parkinsonian tremor does not do; tone is normal.

key_clinical_evidence: Positive signs: collapsing weakness of both legs, tremor entrainment, and distractibility of the tremor and of leg strength; the Hoover sign is equivocal.
After 8 months of severe weakness, tone, bulk, reflexes and plantar responses are normal and there are no fasciculations.
Video-EEG recorded two habitual events (7 minutes of irregular shaking with eyes closed; 2 minutes of hand tremor) without ictal change.
Brain and spine MRI, nerve conduction studies and bloods were normal as an outpatient; repeating them answers no new question.
Duloxetine, cyclobenzaprine and sumatriptan form a serotonergic combination worth reviewing.
Stressors before onset and the abuse history are context, neither required nor sufficient for the diagnosis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A second-degree relative with MS barely changes risk; the positive signs, normal reflexes and plantars, and the normal outpatient MRI answer the question.
red_herrings.data_point: Maternal aunt with multiple sclerosis, and a referral question of MS versus inflammatory myelopathy
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchoring on demyelination and repeating the MRI or performing a lumbar puncture
red_herrings.location: Family history and history of present illness

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: One equivocal sign does not negate the others: collapsing weakness, tremor entrainment and distractibility are positive.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Concluding that no positive functional sign is present and continuing to investigate

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Fibromyalgia does not cause give-way paralysis, entraining tremor or convulsive-looking events; these are functional and treatable.
red_herrings.data_point: Rheumatology attribution of the weakness to severe fibromyalgia
red_herrings.intended_effect: Accepting fibromyalgia as the explanation and missing the functional diagnosis and its treatment

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Psychiatric comorbidity neither establishes nor refutes FND; it is a treatment target, and the diagnosis rests on the signs and the event semiology.
red_herrings.data_point: Depression, generalized anxiety disorder and childhood physical abuse
red_herrings.intended_effect: Premature anchoring on a psychological label without positive signs, or dismissing the disorder because she is anxious

findings.result: Hip flexion, knee extension and ankle movements give way bilaterally after an initial full effort.
During rhythmic tapping with the right hand, the left hand tremor briefly takes on the tapping frequency and then stops.
The hand tremor stops when she talks about her children, and she repositions her legs in bed with more force than on formal testing.
Equivocal: involuntary hip extension is weak on the right and questionably present on the left during contralateral hip flexion against resistance; not counted.
Normal tone and bulk in the legs, reflexes 2+ and symmetric, flexor plantar responses, no clonus or fasciculations.

Loss of all sensory modalities from the inguinal creases with a sharp midline split, vibration absent over the legs but felt at the sternum and iliac crests, and a dragging, non-patterned gait with sway but no fall when released; not counted as rule-in signs.

clinical_assessment.impression: Positive signs of functional weakness and tremor: collapsing weakness of both legs, tremor entrainment and distractibility. The Hoover sign is equivocal. The pattern is inconsistent with a structural lesion.

interactions: Duloxetine + cyclobenzaprine + sumatriptan: additive serotonergic effect; risk of serotonin syndrome (tremor, clonus, agitation, autonomic instability). Use the lowest effective doses and monitor; avoid adding further serotonergic agents.
Pregabalin + cyclobenzaprine: additive CNS depression (sedation, dizziness, impaired balance).
Duloxetine + ibuprofen: increased risk of gastrointestinal bleeding (SNRI impairs platelet serotonin uptake; NSAID mucosal injury).
general.proposed: Duloxetine 60 mg once daily; Pregabalin 150 mg twice daily; Cyclobenzaprine 10 mg at bedtime as needed; Sumatriptan 50 mg as needed for migraine, up to 9 per month; Cholecalciferol 2000 IU once daily; Ibuprofen 400 mg as needed, up to three times daily
general.summary: Three interactions: a serotonergic combination (duloxetine, cyclobenzaprine, sumatriptan), additive sedation (pregabalin, cyclobenzaprine) and bleeding risk (duloxetine, ibuprofen).
warnings: Duloxetine: tremor is a recognised adverse effect.
Pregabalin: dizziness, somnolence, ataxia and blurred vision, dose-related.

activating_procedures.hyperventilation: Three minutes performed. No change in background and no clinical event.
activating_procedures.photic_stimulation: Normal photic driving response. No photoparoxysmal response.

artifacts.impact: Intermittently obscured the temporal channels; cerebral activity remained interpretable throughout

background.posterior_dominant_rhythm: 9.5 Hz well-organized alpha rhythm, symmetric, reactive to eye opening
background.recording: 72-hour inpatient video-EEG monitoring, 21 scalp electrodes (10-20 system) with time-locked video
background.sleep_features: Vertex waves, sleep spindles and K-complexes in stage N2 sleep; normal sleep architecture

findings.morphology: Irregular, asynchronous shaking of all four limbs varying in amplitude, eyes closed throughout. The posterior dominant rhythm and waking background persisted under muscle artifact; no rhythmic ictal pattern before, during or after the event and no postictal slowing.
Coarse tremor of both hands, variable in frequency and amplitude. Low-amplitude muscle artifact over a normal waking background; no rhythmic ictal pattern.

eeg.impression: This is a NORMAL video-EEG. 2 habitual events were recorded (a 7-minute episode of irregular shaking of all four limbs with eyes closed; a 2-minute episode of bilateral hand tremor) without ictal EEG change before, during or after the events; the posterior dominant rhythm persisted during the events. No interictal epileptiform discharges. No electrographic seizures.
eeg.limitations: Muscle artifact during the shaking event intermittently obscured the temporal channels.

results.finding: Diagnosis of functional neurological disorder rests on positive clinical features such as the Hoover sign, tremor entrainment and functional seizure semiology, not on the exclusion of other disease; treatment combines explanation, physiotherapy and psychological therapy.
results.source: Espay AJ et al. JAMA Neurol 2018;75:1132-1141

results.finding: Motor signs such as the Hoover sign, hip abductor sign, drift without pronation and dragging gait have high specificity; sensory signs such as midline splitting have low specificity.
results.source: Daum C et al. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2014;85:180-190

results.finding: Defines levels of certainty for psychogenic nonepileptic seizures; the documented level requires a typical event recorded on video-EEG without ictal EEG change.
results.source: LaFrance WC Jr et al. Epilepsia 2013;54:2005-2018

results.finding: For functional seizures: assess for co-occurring epilepsy and psychiatric disorders, taper antiseizure medication without another indication, avoid benzodiazepines, and offer psychological therapy, which is possibly effective.
CBT added to standardised medical care did not reduce dissociative seizure frequency at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured CBT.
results.source: Goldstein LH et al. Lancet Psychiatry 2020;7:491-505

results.finding: Specialist physiotherapy for functional motor disorder was not superior to community neurological physiotherapy on physical function at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured it.
results.source: Nielsen G et al. Lancet Neurol 2024;23:675-686

results.finding: About 4% of patients diagnosed with conversion symptoms since 1970 later received another diagnosis.

functional neurological disorder diagnos.summary: Guideline and trial evidence supports a positive clinical diagnosis of functional neurological disorder, video-EEG confirmation of functional seizures, tapering of unneeded antiseizure drugs and benzodiazepines, and physiotherapy and psychological treatment whose trial effects on primary outcomes were modest.

additional_observations: Technique: T1, T2, FLAIR, DWI/ADC and SWI without intravenous contrast. Comparison: outpatient brain MRI earlier in the illness.
No periventricular, juxtacortical or infratentorial white matter lesion.
Normal ventricles and sulci. Normal hippocampi.
mri.impression: Normal non-contrast brain MRI, unchanged from the outpatient study. No acute intracranial abnormality.

patient.history_present_illness:
Mrs. Patterson is a 40-year-old right-handed woman with a complex medical history including fibromyalgia, chronic pain, anxiety, and depression, who is admitted for evaluation of progressive bilateral lower extremity weakness that has rendered her wheelchair-dependent over the past 8 months. She reports that the weakness began insidiously approximately 8 months ago with a sensation of heaviness in both legs, initially more prominent on the right. Over the ensuing weeks, she noticed increasing difficulty climbing stairs, followed by difficulty walking on flat surfaces. By three months into the illness, she required a cane, and by five months she transitioned to a wheelchair, which she now uses full-time.

She describes the weakness as constant but fluctuating in severity from day to day, with some days being slightly better than others without clear pattern. She denies any preceding infection, vaccination, or trauma. She also reports complete numbness in both legs from the groin down, describing it as though her legs do not belong to her. She reports episodes of whole-body shaking lasting 5 to 15 minutes that began approximately 4 months ago, occurring 2 to 3 times per week. During these episodes she reports retained awareness and ability to hear those around her, though she sometimes closes her eyes. Her husband states the shaking is irregular and appears to vary in intensity. On one occasion he tried gently holding her arms during an episode and the shaking stopped momentarily before resuming in her legs.

She has also developed an intermittent coarse tremor in both hands over the past 2 months, which she notices primarily when she is anxious or fatigued. She has seen multiple physicians over the past 8 months. An outpatient neurologist obtained a brain and spine MRI which were normal, routine nerve conduction studies that were normal, and basic blood work that was unremarkable. She was referred with a tentative diagnosis of possible multiple sclerosis versus inflammatory myelopathy versus motor neuron disease, though all workup has been negative. A rheumatology consultation attributed her symptoms to severe fibromyalgia, but the referring neurologist felt the degree of weakness was disproportionate to that diagnosis and referred her for inpatient evaluation. The patient is frustrated with the lack of a diagnosis and expresses fear that she has a progressive neurodegenerative disease. She tearfully states that her life has changed completely and she feels she is a burden to her family.

neurological_exam.additional: Hoover sign was tested and is equivocal — involuntary hip extension is weak on the right but questionably present on the left during contralateral hip flexion against resistance. Tremor entrainment test: patient has intermittent coarse bilateral hand tremor at rest that is variable in frequency and amplitude; when asked to perform a rhythmic tapping task with the right hand, the left hand tremor entrains to the tapping frequency briefly before stopping entirely. The tremor is distractible — it ceases when the patient is engaged in conversation about her children.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Rapid alternating movements normal in upper extremities. Heel-to-shin testing is difficult to assess as patient reports inability to lift legs adequately, but when performed with examiner assistance, no dysmetria is apparent.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, reactive to light 3 mm to 2 mm bilaterally. Visual fields full to confrontation. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus or diplopia. Facial sensation intact bilaterally to light touch and pinprick. Face symmetric at rest and with activation. Hearing intact bilaterally to finger rub. Palate elevates symmetrically. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius 5/5 bilaterally. Tongue midline without atrophy or fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Patient states she is unable to stand or walk. When assisted to standing with two-person support, she demonstrates marked sway with irregular, non-patterned truncal movements. She reaches for support but catches herself with movements that require significant strength and coordination. She does not fall when unexpectedly released (with spotter present). When asked to walk, she takes several steps with a dragging, non-pyramidal pattern of bilateral leg movement, inconsistent with any recognized neurological gait pattern.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Affect is flat but cooperative. Speech is fluent without dysarthria or aphasia. Naming, repetition, and comprehension intact. Attention normal on digit span (6 forward, 4 backward). Memory 3/3 registration, 2/3 recall at 5 minutes (recalled third with category cue). Clock drawing normal. Fund of knowledge appropriate for education level. No evidence of thought disorder.
neurological_exam.motor: Upper extremities: Normal bulk and tone. Strength 5/5 bilaterally in deltoids, biceps, triceps, wrist extensors/flexors, and grip. No pronator drift. Lower extremities: Normal bulk. Tone is normal without spasticity or rigidity. On formal testing, hip flexors 2/5 bilaterally, knee extensors 3/5 bilaterally, ankle dorsiflexors 3/5 bilaterally, ankle plantarflexors 2/5 bilaterally. However, strength testing demonstrates give-way pattern with initial full effort followed by sudden collapse. When the patient is distracted during conversation, spontaneous leg movements are observed including repositioning legs in bed with apparently greater force than demonstrated on formal testing. No muscle atrophy. No fasciculations.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Upper extremities: 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, and brachioradialis bilaterally. Lower extremities: 2+ and symmetric at patellae and Achilles bilaterally. Plantar responses are flexor (downgoing) bilaterally. No clonus. No Hoffman sign.
neurological_exam.sensory: Reports complete loss of sensation to light touch, pinprick, temperature, proprioception, and vibration from the bilateral inguinal creases distally in a non-dermatomal distribution. The sensory loss has a sharp midline split at the trunk. Vibration sense is reported absent over the legs but is felt normally at the sternum and over the iliac crests. Double simultaneous stimulation testing is normal in upper extremities.
